\chapter{Introducing Yourself}
\label{ch:introductions}
\hlchaptermodality{2}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can introduce myself in Gujarati, give my name, and understand the other person's name.}

Complete GU-C02-practice, the canonical closing checkpoint, and demonstrate the chapter promise: introduce myself in Gujarati, give my name, and understand the other person's name.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\gu{નામ}]{\gu{નામ} (nām) — \textquotedblleft{}name,\textquotedblright{} a word older than Europe}

\label{lesson:GU-C02-naam}



\begin{quote}
The first word of the introduction — and a bridge between India and Europe.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\gu{ન}} (\emph{na}) + \textbf{\gu{ા}} (long \emph{ā}) + \textbf{\gu{મ}} (\emph{ma}) $\to$ \textbf{\gu{નામ}} (\emph{nām}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\gu{નામ}} (\emph{nām}, \textquotedblleft{}name\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Sanskrit \textbf{\gu{નામન્}} (\emph{nāman}), from Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*h\textsubscript{3}nómn} (its final \emph{n} syllabic) — the same root as English \textbf{name}, Latin \emph{nōmen} ($\to$ \textbf{noun}), Greek \emph{onoma}, and Hindi \emph{nām}. Gujarati \emph{nām} and English \emph{name} are cousins from before either language existed.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nām\textquotedblright{}
  \item the family — \emph{nām} / English \emph{name} / Latin \emph{nōmen}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What root is \emph{nām} from, and its English cousin? (Sanskrit \emph{nāman} / PIE \emph{*h\textsubscript{3}nómn}; English \textbf{name}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\gu{મારું}]{\gu{મારું} (mārũ) — \textquotedblleft{}my,\textquotedblright{} and gender again}

\label{lesson:GU-C02-maarun}



\begin{quote}
The word that makes the name yours — and, like \emph{sārũ}, it changes with gender.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\gu{મા}} (\emph{mā}) + \textbf{\gu{રું}} (\emph{rũ}, with the nasal) $\to$ \textbf{\gu{મારું}} (\emph{mārũ}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\gu{મારું}} (\emph{mārũ}, \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{}) is on the first-person root \textbf{ma-} — the same \emph{ma-/me-} behind English \textbf{me}, \textbf{my}, \textbf{mine}, Latin \emph{meus}, and Hindi \emph{merā}. Gujarati's \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{} and English's \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{} are, at the root, one word.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{} agrees in all three genders}]
Because \emph{nām} (\textquotedblleft{}name\textquotedblright{}) is \textbf{neuter}, \textquotedblleft{}my name\textquotedblright{} is \textbf{\gu{મારું} \gu{નામ}} (\emph{mārũ nām}) — the neuter \emph{mārũ}. The full set:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\gu{મારો}} (\emph{māro}) — masculine (e.g. \emph{māro dēsh}, \textquotedblleft{}my country\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\gu{મારી}} (\emph{mārī}) — feminine (e.g. \emph{mārī bhāṣā}, \textquotedblleft{}my language\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\gu{મારું}} (\emph{mārũ}) — \textbf{neuter} (e.g. \emph{mārũ nām}, \textquotedblleft{}my name\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

Every possessive works this way — three forms, chosen by the noun's gender. It is the thread you first pulled in Chapter 1's \emph{sārũ}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the three — \emph{māro} (m.) / \emph{mārī} (f.) / \emph{mārũ} (n.)
  \item \textquotedblleft{}my name\textquotedblright{} and why (\emph{mārũ nām} — \emph{nām} is neuter)
  \item the m- family (\emph{mārũ}, English \emph{me}, \emph{my})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which form of \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{} goes with \emph{nām}, and why? (\emph{Mārũ} — the neuter, because \emph{nām} is a neuter noun.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\gu{છે}]{\gu{છે} (chhe) — \textquotedblleft{}is,\textquotedblright{} a copula all Gujarati's own}

\label{lesson:GU-C02-chhe}



\begin{quote}
The little verb \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{} — and here it is a word you will \emph{not} recognise from Hindi.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\gu{છ}} (\emph{chha}, a breathy \emph{ch}) + \textbf{\gu{ે}} (the \emph{e}-sign) $\to$ \textbf{\gu{છે}} (\emph{chhe}). One syllable.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\gu{છે}} (\emph{chhe}, \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{}) is Gujarati's \textbf{copula} — and, unusually, it is \emph{not} the \emph{hai} of Hindi or the \emph{asti} of Sanskrit. It grew from an Old Gujarati form (\emph{achhaï}) along its own path, so it is one of the words that most quickly marks a sentence as \emph{Gujarati} rather than Hindi. Its forms run: \textbf{\gu{હું} \gu{છું}} (\emph{hũ chhũ}, \textquotedblleft{}I am\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{\gu{તું} \gu{છે}} (\emph{tũ chhe}, \textquotedblleft{}you are\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{\gu{તે} \gu{છે}} (\emph{te chhe}, \textquotedblleft{}he/she/it is\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{\gu{તમે} \gu{છો}} (\emph{tame chho}, \textquotedblleft{}you are,\textquotedblright{} respectful).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the verb goes last}]
Gujarati is \textbf{subject–object–verb}, like all its Indo-Aryan sisters: \textquotedblleft{}my name Arun \textbf{is}.\textquotedblright{} \emph{Chhe} sits at the end of the sentence, where English puts \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{} in the middle.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}chhe\textquotedblright{}
  \item the copula set — \emph{hũ chhũ} (I am), \emph{tame chho} (you are), \emph{te chhe} (is)
  \item what makes \emph{chhe} special (it's Gujarati's own, not Hindi's \emph{hai})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{chhe}, and how does it differ from Hindi? (Gujarati's copula, \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{}; it is not Hindi's \emph{hai} — a distinctively Gujarati word.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\gu{મારું} \gu{નામ} … \gu{છે}]{\gu{મારું} \gu{નામ} … \gu{છે} (mārũ nām … chhe) — \textquotedblleft{}my name is…\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GU-C02-maarun-naam-chhe}



\begin{quote}
Three atoms you now own, assembled into a first sentence.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The two words — assembled}
\textbf{\gu{મારું}} (my, neuter) + \textbf{\gu{નામ}} (name) + your name + \textbf{\gu{છે}} (is) = \textbf{mārũ nām … chhe}, \textquotedblleft{}my name is…\textquotedblright{} \emph{Mārũ nām Arun chhe.} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}My name is Arun.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the verb goes last}]
Gujarati keeps the verb at the \textbf{end} — \textquotedblleft{}my name Arun \textbf{is}.\textquotedblright{} Note too that \emph{mārũ} is neuter to agree with \emph{nām} (neuter): the agreement you learned two lessons ago is already doing its quiet work.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}mārũ nām … chhe\textquotedblright{} with your name
  \item why \emph{mārũ} (neuter) and where \emph{chhe} sits (agrees with \emph{nām}; verb last)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give your name in Gujarati, and say where the verb goes. (\emph{Mārũ nām … chhe}; the verb \emph{chhe} is last.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\gu{તમને} \gu{મળીને} \gu{આનંદ} \gu{થયો}]{\gu{તમને} \gu{મળીને} \gu{આનંદ} \gu{થયો} (tamne maḷīne ānand thayo) — \textquotedblleft{}pleased to meet you\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GU-C02-anand}



\begin{quote}
The warm close of an introduction — a word that means bliss itself.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
The key word is \textbf{\gu{આનંદ}} (\emph{ānand}): \textbf{\gu{આ}} + \textbf{\gu{ન}} + \textbf{\gu{ં}} (the nasal) + \textbf{\gu{દ}} (\emph{da}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\gu{તમને} \gu{મળીને} \gu{આનંદ} \gu{થયો}} = \textbf{\gu{તમને}} (\emph{tamne}, \textquotedblleft{}to you\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\gu{મળીને}} (\emph{maḷīne}, \textquotedblleft{}having met\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\gu{આનંદ} \gu{થયો}} (\emph{ānand thayo}, \textquotedblleft{}joy happened\textquotedblright{}) — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{having met you, joy happened}.\textquotedblright{} The key word \textbf{\gu{આનંદ}} (\emph{ānand}, \textquotedblleft{}joy, bliss\textquotedblright{}) is \textbf{Sanskrit} — \emph{ā-} (\textquotedblleft{}fully\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{nand} (\textquotedblleft{}to rejoice\textquotedblright{}) — the \emph{ānanda} of \emph{sat-cit-ānanda} (\textquotedblleft{}being-consciousness-bliss\textquotedblright{}), and a common Gujarati name. So a simple greeting reaches, as Sanskrit did, for the word for the deepest happiness.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}tamne maḷīne ānand thayo\textquotedblright{}
  \item the key word and its meaning (\emph{ānand}, \textquotedblleft{}joy/bliss\textquotedblright{})
  \item what it's built from (\emph{ā-} \textquotedblleft{}fully\textquotedblright{} + \emph{nand} \textquotedblleft{}to rejoice\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the phrase literally say, and what is \emph{ānand}? (\textquotedblleft{}Having met you, joy happened\textquotedblright{}; Sanskrit \emph{ānanda}, \textquotedblleft{}bliss.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\gu{તું} / \gu{તમે}]{\gu{તું} / \gu{તમે} (tũ / tame) — \textquotedblleft{}you,\textquotedblright{} familiar and respectful}

\label{lesson:GU-C02-tu-tame}



\begin{quote}
To ask a name you need \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} — and Gujarati grades respect the way French does.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\gu{તું}} (\emph{tũ}): \textbf{\gu{ત}} (\emph{ta}) + the \emph{u}-sign + nasal. \textbf{\gu{તમે}} (\emph{tame}): \textbf{\gu{ત}} + \textbf{\gu{મ}} + \textbf{\gu{ે}}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\gu{તું}} (\emph{tũ}, familiar \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Sanskrit \emph{tvam}, from PIE \textbf{*tū} — the same root as English archaic \textbf{thou}, Latin \emph{tū}, French \emph{tu}, and Hindi \emph{tū}. \textbf{\gu{તમે}} (\emph{tame}, respectful \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{}) is grammatically plural — courtesy-by-plural, like French \emph{vous} and Hindi \emph{āp}. For a first meeting, use \textbf{\gu{તમે}}; it takes the plural copula \emph{chho} (\emph{tame … chho}).
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}tũ\textquotedblright{} (familiar) and \textquotedblleft{}tame\textquotedblright{} (respectful)
  \item the English cousin of \emph{tũ} (\textbf{thou})
  \item which you use on first meeting (\emph{tame})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} is respectful, and what English word is \emph{tũ} cousin to? (\emph{Tame}; archaic \textbf{thou}, from PIE \emph{*tū}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\gu{શું}]{\gu{શું} (shũ) — \textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GU-C02-shun}



\begin{quote}
The question-word — and the one Gujarati question that does \emph{not} start with k-.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\gu{શ}} (\emph{sha}) + the \emph{u}-sign + nasal $\to$ \textbf{\gu{શું}} (\emph{shũ}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\gu{શું}} (\emph{shũ}, \textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{}) descends, by a winding road, from the Sanskrit interrogative stem \textbf{\gu{ક}-} (\emph{ka-}, PIE \textbf{*k\textsuperscript{w}o-}) — the root behind English \textbf{what}, Latin \emph{quis}, and Hindi \emph{kyā}. Most of Gujarati's questions still show that \textbf{k-} plainly — \textbf{\gu{કેમ}} (\emph{kem}, how), \textbf{\gu{કોણ}} (\emph{kōṇ}, who), \textbf{\gu{ક્યાં}} (\emph{kyā̃}, where), \textbf{\gu{ક્યારે}} (\emph{kyāre}, when) — but \textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{} wore down into this \emph{sh-} form. So \emph{shũ} is the odd cousin in a \emph{k-} family.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}shũ\textquotedblright{}
  \item the k- question family it belongs to (\emph{kem, kōṇ, kyā̃, kyāre})
  \item its distant English cousin (\emph{what})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{shũ} mean, and what root does it share with English \emph{what}? (\textquotedblleft{}What\textquotedblright{}; the interrogative \emph{ka-} / PIE \emph{*k\textsuperscript{w}o-} — worn to \emph{sh-} in Gujarati.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\gu{તમારું} \gu{નામ} \gu{શું} \gu{છે}?]{\gu{તમારું} \gu{નામ} \gu{શું} \gu{છે}? (tamārũ nām shũ chhe?) — \textquotedblleft{}what's your name?\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GU-C02-tamarun-naam-shun-chhe}



\begin{quote}
Turn the introduction around — ask, instead of tell.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The two words — assembled}
\textbf{\gu{તમારું}} (\emph{tamārũ}, \textquotedblleft{}your,\textquotedblright{} the respectful possessive from \emph{tame}, neuter to match \emph{nām}) + \textbf{\gu{નામ}} (name) + \textbf{\gu{શું}} (what) + \textbf{\gu{છે}} (is) $\to$ literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{your name what is?}\textquotedblright{} Gujarati keeps the verb last and drops the question-word \emph{shũ} into the object slot.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: answering, and the familiar form}]
Answer with the sentence you built: \emph{Mārũ nām Arun chhe.} The familiar version swaps \emph{tamārũ} for \textbf{\gu{તારું}} (\emph{tārũ}, \textquotedblleft{}your,\textquotedblright{} from \emph{tũ}): \emph{tārũ nām shũ chhe?} Note \emph{mārũ / tārũ / tamārũ} — \textquotedblleft{}my / your / your (resp.)\textquotedblright{} — all take the neuter \emph{-ũ} before \emph{nām}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the respectful question — \emph{tamārũ nām shũ chhe?}
  \item answer it — \emph{mārũ nām … chhe}
  \item the familiar \textquotedblleft{}your\textquotedblright{} (\emph{tārũ})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Ask \textquotedblleft{}what's your name?\textquotedblright{} respectfully. (\emph{Tamārũ nām shũ chhe?}; the verb \emph{chhe} is last.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Chapter 2 — The introduction exchange}

\label{lesson:GU-C02-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. The whole introduction, assembled from atoms you now own.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}My name is Mira.\textquotedblright{} — \emph{mārũ nām Mira chhe.}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}What's your name?\textquotedblright{} — \emph{tamārũ nām shũ chhe?}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}My name is Arun.\textquotedblright{} — \emph{mārũ nām Arun chhe.}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Pleased to meet you.\textquotedblright{} — \emph{tamne maḷīne ānand thayo.}
\end{itemize}

\begin{cousinweb}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}name,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}my,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{} (\emph{nām}, \emph{mārũ}, \emph{chhe})
  \item the two \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} levels (\emph{tũ} / \emph{tame})
  \item \textquotedblleft{}what,\textquotedblright{} and where the verb sits (\emph{shũ}; the verb is last)
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — roots you now carry}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{nām} $\leftarrow$ Sanskrit \emph{nāman} $\to$ English \textbf{name}
  \item \emph{mārũ} $\leftarrow$ \emph{ma-} $\to$ English \textbf{my}; agrees in three genders (\emph{māro/mārī/mārũ})
  \item \emph{chhe} — Gujarati's own copula (not Hindi's \emph{hai})
  \item \emph{shũ} $\leftarrow$ \emph{ka-} $\to$ English \emph{what}; \emph{tũ} $\leftarrow$ \emph{*tū} $\to$ \emph{thou}
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Introduce yourself and ask a stranger's name in Gujarati. (\emph{Mārũ nām … chhe. Tamārũ nām shũ chhe?})
\end{tcolorbox}
